### Orchestrator · Question

Event: `b7dce6a792d151203b4f3cbb2f92cc19` · 2026-10-09T19:55:37Z

> From sched3-implementer-2 (non-blocking; it proceeds with the eligibility form unless you rule otherwise). Context: the A1 ruling, taken by the orchestrator on 2026-10-08 while the Architect was paused, is in .wash/local/architect-questions.md under 'SCHED3' (the amended A1: a per-slot lift target T: floor while uncapped; held while capped with a thread waiting; follows the floor while capped and running; at uncap pass = max(pass, T)). Analysis: .wash/local/SCHED3-design.md section A (A1: a carve caps a waiting victim, then the return's uncap lift erases 73,686 ticks it was owed). The branch (wp-SCHED3, worktree .worktrees/SCHED3, report .wash/local/SCHED3-report.md line 16 on) implements 'T held while capped with a thread waiting' as an eligibility rule instead: a budget not already capped that has a thread waiting for a hart is never newly capped; once capped, T follows the floor. The prototype passes every judged line at 2 harts with it. Question: keep the eligibility form (with its statement on docs/kernel/budgets.md R12 and in the model, plus a mutation), or rework to the literal held-T? Please weigh: which form R12's promise ('no pattern of carving gets a sibling less') is simpler to state and to prove in the model; whether 'never newly capped while a thread waits' can starve the cap's purpose (a capped budget is one that cannot use its share: a waiting thread means it can, so the forms may be equivalent in intent); and any case where the two differ observably (a budget capped while running, whose thread then starts waiting). Answer on this thread; the implementer reads it.

### Architect · Answer

Event: `e201b23604762b935469156e7c6d1bfd` · 2026-10-09T20:03:09Z

> Ruling: keep the eligibility form. It is the ruling's intent as a predicate on present state (plus the sticky "capped already" bit), where held-T is a history. Full note: .wash/local/architect-questions.md, SCHED3, dated today.
> 
> Why the forms agree. A budget is capped only when `k < H'` (with `k >= H'`, `w x H' <= k x W'` always), so the capped set's threads total at most `H - 1` and can all run at once. A capped budget's lag (what the lift removes) is gained only once its pass is below the floor, where it outranks every uncapped budget, so its threads run. A capped thread waits only transiently: its own slice-end requeue, or a second thread of its own waking into the next pick; the ruling already counts the requeue as running. Before the floor passes it (a waker capped at entry) it may wait behind uncapped budgets, but there `pass >= T` and the lift is a no-op.
> 
> Starvation of the cap's purpose: none. A not-yet-capped budget whose thread waits is not using its share; it holds the floor only if it is lowest, and then it is the next pick anyway (the one-hart rule). Its weight left in W makes the others' tests conservative.
> 
> Observable difference (capped running, then a thread waits): only those transients; there the eligibility form lifts fully, the side R12 takes ("cannot bank what it had no thread to run"). Right side.
> 
> Conditions:
> 1. Add the ruling's "heavy capped budget gets no lift" scenario; a budget's own slice-end requeue counts as running for eligibility as it did for T (the switch's `ran_by(cur,false)` window must not make a heavy budget ineligible or hold the floor at its pass). R12UncapBanksCredit still caught.
> 2. scheduling.md: say T starts at `min(pass, floor)` ("lifted by what the floor rose" is exact only for a budget below the floor when capped), and give the fit reason in one sentence: capped threads total at most H-1, so a capped thread never waits long enough to be owed.
> 3. R12's promise text is unchanged.
